hints: Look closely at Fig. 3.1 at the bottom part of the TKR inside the cell - what shapes do you see where ATP and the intracellular protein fit?
Think about what determines that shape in a protein and why only molecules with a matching shape can bind there to react.
walkthrough:
See The Lock And Key In Fig. 3.1**
Look at the left diagram. The enzyme component has two little hollows. The ATP shape and the oval intracellular protein shape fit exactly into those hollows. On the right, after signalling, you can see them sitting in the enzyme. That hollow is the active site.

Why Only Those Substrates Fit**
A protein gets its 3D shape from its tertiary structure, the way its amino acid chain folds. That folding creates an active site with a very precise shape and arrangement. Only substrates with a complementary shape, here ATP and the intracellular protein, can bind. That is what makes the enzyme specific to one reaction.
Final answer: The enzyme component has an active site with a specific shape / tertiary structure that is complementary to its substrates, ATP and the intracellular protein.

hints: Compare the solid and dashed curves in Fig. 3.2 at low ATP on the left side, around 0.1 to 1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ - which curve is lower?
Now follow both curves to the right to high ATP, around 100 to 1000 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ - what happens to the gap between them and the final maximum rate?
Recall what happens to Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition when more substrate can outcompete the inhibitor for the active site.
walkthrough:
GNF-5 Lowers Activity At Low Substrate**
With no GNF-5 at 0.1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP, activity is about 2 arbitrary units, but with GNF-5 it is only about 0.4. At 1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ the solid curve is about 7 and the dashed curve is only about 2. So GNF-5 is inhibiting the enzyme.

Inhibition Is Overcome By More ATP**
As you move right on the x-axis the gap closes. By 10 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ the curves are much closer, and by 100 to 1000 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ both reach the same maximum rate, Vmax of 10 arbitrary units. That is the hallmark of competitive inhibition: high substrate outcompetes inhibitor for the active site.

Km Increases, Vmax Stays Same**
Because more ATP is needed to reach the same rate, the Michaelis constant Km is higher with GNF-5. Same Vmax plus higher Km plus reduced effect at high substrate proves competitive inhibition.

Final answer: At low ATP concentration rate is lower with GNF-5; as ATP concentration increases the inhibitory effect decreases; Vmax is the same at 10 arbitrary units with and without GNF-5; Km is higher with GNF-5, e.g. more $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP needed to reach half Vmax.

hints: Compare only the solid curves (no GNF-5) in Fig. 3.2 and Fig. 3.3 at the far left, at 0.1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP - what is the activity value in each?
walkthrough:
Compare Solid Curves Like With Like**
Ignore the dashed lines for this part. In Fig. 3.2 the solid TKR curve starts at about 2 arbitrary units at 0.1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP. In Fig. 3.3 the solid T315L curve starts at 0 at 0.1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP. The whole T315L curve is shifted right, so it needs more ATP to reach half maximum, meaning higher Km, although both eventually reach Vmax of 10.
Final answer: Without GNF-5, T315L has 0 activity at 0.1 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP compared to about 2 for normal TKR, and has a higher Km but reaches the same Vmax.

hints: Compare the dashed curves at the far right in Fig. 3.2 and Fig. 3.3, at 100 to 1000 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP - does the dashed line still reach 10 in both figures?
Think about what type of inhibition lowers Vmax so it cannot be overcome by adding more substrate, and check if the gap at low ATP is big or small for T315L.
walkthrough:
Vmax Is No Longer Reached**
In Fig. 3.2 with GNF-5 the dashed TKR curve still climbs to 10 arbitrary units at high ATP. In Fig. 3.3 with GNF-5 the dashed T315L curve levels off at about 8.5 to 8.7 and never reaches 10, even at 1000 $\mu\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ATP. When extra substrate cannot overcome inhibition, Vmax is lowered.

Change To Non-Competitive Behaviour**
Lowered Vmax means GNF-5 is now acting like a non-competitive inhibitor of the mutant, binding elsewhere and not directly competing with ATP. Also the solid and dashed lines for T315L are very close at low ATP, so GNF-5 has much less effect there than it did on normal TKR. The mutation has changed how the drug interacts with the enzyme.

Final answer: With GNF-5, T315L does not reach the normal Vmax of 10, only about 8.7 arbitrary units, whereas TKR with GNF-5 does reach 10; GNF-5 acts as a non-competitive inhibitor of T315L and has less effect at low ATP concentrations.
